system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was readmitted for failure to thrive, fever, productive cough, and worsening abdominal pain around her gastrostomy tube. She had been recently discharged after a prior admission for radiation-induced esophagitis and G-tube placement. Imaging revealed new right lower lobe consolidation consistent with healthcare-associated pneumonia, for which she was treated with intravenous vancomycin and cefepime. Her abdominal pain and feed leakage were attributed to a mechanical issue with the pigtail G-tube, which was successfully replaced with a balloon-type MIC feeding tube, leading to marked improvement. Her esophagitis was managed with lansoprazole and oral rest, and her chronic pain was controlled with morphine while discontinuing sedating medications like nortriptyline. She completed antibiotic therapy, showed clinical resolution of infection, and was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with plans for outpatient GI and rheumatology follow-up.

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST RADIOGRAPHS

HISTORY:  Malaise, wheezing and low-grade fever.

COMPARISONS:  Chest radiographs are available from ___ and more
recent chest CT studies from ___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Chest, PA and lateral view.

FINDINGS:  The lung volumes are again low.  The heart is mildly enlarged.  The
mediastinal and hilar contours appear unchanged.  There is similar moderate to
severe relative elevation of the right hemidiaphragm compared to the left. 
Compared to the prior radiographs there is increased widespread opacification
of the right upper lobe which is also more prominent than on the more recent
of the two chest CT studies.  This appearance is concerning for pneumonia
superimposed on chronic scarring.  There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The patient is status post bilateral shoulder replacements.

IMPRESSION: New opacification of the right upper lobe worrisome for pneumonia
superimposed on more chronic changes.

INDICATION:  Profuse diarrhea and signs of obstruction, evaluate for
obstruction or colitis.

COMPARISON:  ___ CTA chest, abdomen and pelvis.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT axial images were obtained from the dome of the liver to the
pubic symphysis after the uneventful administration of 130 mL of Omnipaque and
oral contrast.  Coronal and sagittal reformations were provided and reviewed.

DLP:  872.02 mGy-cm.

FINDINGS:  The imaged lung bases are clear, without pleural effusion or
pneumothorax.  The imaged portion of the heart is unremarkable.  Aortic,
mitral valve and coronary calcifications are seen.

The liver enhances homogeneously without focal lesions.  The gallbladder is
collapsed and there is no intrahepatic biliary duct dilatation.  The spleen,
pancreas, and adrenal glands are normal.  The kidneys enhance symmetrically
and excrete contrast without hydronephrosis.  A percutaneous gastrostomy tube
is seen with its tube looping in the stomach and terminating in the second
part of the duodenum.  The stomach and small bowel are normal.  The colon is
fluid filled but without wall thickening or dilation.  There is no
retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy.  There are dense calcifications
seen throughout the aorta and at the origin of the celiac artery, without
aneurysmal dilatation.  The splenic vein, portal vein, superior mesenteric
vein are patent.  There is no free air or free fluid.

PELVIS:  The bladder and uterus are normal.  There is mild sigmoid
diverticulosis, without diverticulitis.  There is no free pelvic fluid.  Ring
hypodensities seen around the urethra are unchanged and consistent with
urethral diverticula.

BONES:  There are no suspicious osseous lesions.  Again seen is grade II
anterolisthesis of L4 on L5.  Degenerative changes of the lower lumbar spine
are marked by vacuum phenomenon and osteophyte formation, at L4-L5.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Fluid filled colon without wall thickening or dilation.

2.  Percutaneous G-tube loops in the stomach and ends in the duodenum;
accordingly the jejunal tube has pulled back and is malpositioned.

3.  Sigmoid diverticulosis without diverticulitis.

NOTE: These findings were discussed with Dr. ___ by Dr. ___ on ___ at 1635 via telephone.

PROCEDURE: Gastrojejunostomy tube exchange: ___.

INDICATION:  ___ year-old woman with head and neck cancer, admitted with
diarrhea.  CT showed GJ tube malposition.

RADIOLOGISTS:  Dr. ___ (fellow) performed the procedure.  Dr.
___ (attending physician) was present and supervised throughout the
procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate intravenous sedation was administered via divided doses
of 50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed throughout the total intraservice
time of 30 minutes, during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored.

TECHNIQUE/FINDINGS:

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after explaining the
risks, benefits, and alternatives to the procedure.  The patient was brought
to the angiography suite and positioned supine on the table.  The existing Gj
tube was prepped and draped in a sterile fashion.  A preprocedural huddle and
timeout were performed per ___ protocol.

On initial contrast injection, the tip of the catheter was found to be in the
stomach.  A ___ wire was coiled in the stomach, and the existing GJ tube
was removed.  A Kumpe catheter and the ___ wire were utilized to gain
access to the jejunum.  The ___ wire was replaced with a 0.035 inch
super-stiff Glidewire.  A 16 ___ MIC GJ tube was then advanced over the
Glidewire with the tip in the jejunum.  This was confirmed by contrast
injection.  The balloon was inflated utilizing 8 mL of sterile water mixed
with contrast.

The patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate
complications.  Sterile dressings were applied.

IMPRESSION:

Uncomplicated replacement of a 16 ___ MIC GJ tube.  The tip of the catheter
is in the jejunum.  The tube is ready for use.

ABDOMEN FILM ON ___

HISTORY:  Tracheal cancer, esophagitis, GJ tube repositioned yesterday.  Now
with nausea and vomiting.

FINDINGS:  Residual contrast is seen in the colon.  The enteric tube is seen
projecting over the mid abdomen.  No free air is identified on the decubitus
film.

A negative result does not rule out infection due to other L. pneumophila serogroups or other Legionella species. Furthermore, in infected patients the excretion of antigen in urine may vary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started suddenly last night. I’ve had stomach pain, and I’ve thrown up a few times. The diarrhea is watery and greenish. I haven’t had a fever, but I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you might have vomited some of your pills this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I think so. I couldn’t keep them down. I take a lot of medications—morphine, blood pressure pills, inhalers…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you get back on track with those. You also said you’ve been more short of breath and coughing lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the past week. I’m on antibiotics at home—cefpodoxime—and I’ve been using my inhalers more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We did a chest X-ray today, and it shows a new shadow in your right upper lung. This is concerning for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? Again? I’ve had that before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to treat, but we’ve started you on an antibiotic called levofloxacin. That should help clear it up over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. What about the diarrhea? That’s what brought me in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool, and it’s not a C. difficile infection or any other common bacteria. That’s good news. But we did a CT scan, and it showed something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GJ tube—the feeding tube that goes into your stomach and small intestine—isn’t in the right place. The part that should be in your jejunum has pulled back into your stomach. That could be causing the diarrhea and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. That happened before, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll need to fix it. Interventional radiology will replace the tube tomorrow. In the meantime, we’re holding your tube feeds to let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put me to sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—fentanyl and Versed—to keep you comfortable. It’s a common procedure, and they’ll make sure the new tube is in the right spot with X-ray guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my pain? I’ve been on morphine, and it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on your regular morphine dose. We know you have chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia, so we’ll manage that carefully while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back negative for infections, which confirms our suspicion that the tube feeds were likely causing the diarrhea due to the speed or positioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So once the tube is fixed, I can start feeding again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll start slowly. Nutrition will help us plan the best way—either giving the feedings more slowly or adjusting the rate to prevent diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking… I’d like to try to stop using the tube altogether. Can I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But right now, with your esophageal stricture and history of swallowing issues, it’s safer to keep it. You did well with calories by mouth on two of the three days we checked, so you can eat when you can, and use the tube when you need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just hate being dependent on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology team is about to replace your GJ tube. They’ll make sure it’s in the right place in your jejunum. Any questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I understand. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you’ll feel very relaxed and won’t feel pain. Afterward, you might have some mild discomfort, but we’ll manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. Your new MIC GJ tube is in place, with the tip in the jejunum. We’ll wait a few hours and then start a slow refeed to see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I hope this stops the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had some nausea and vomiting overnight. We did an abdominal X-ray, and there’s no blockage or free air, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt better by this morning. My daughter says I get nauseated often at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s something we’ve noted. We’ll keep monitoring. The tube feeds are running slowly, and we’ll adjust as needed. Your lungs are clearer today—less wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using my inhalers regularly. Is the pneumonia getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your cough is still there, but it may be partly from bronchitis. We lowered your prednisone back to 10 mg since your breathing improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved since stopping and restarting the feeds slowly. We think the speed was contributing to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need to go slow with the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Nutrition recommends either giving one can of Isosource 1.5 three times a day slowly, or running it at 75 mL per hour for 10 hours. You can eat by mouth too—just supplement when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that. What about my follow-up for the esophageal stricture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI is aware. You wanted to delay the endoscopy, and they’ll reschedule it. We’ll make sure you have an appointment before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pneumonia is resolving, the tube is working, and your blood pressure is stable on your usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. You’ll go home with services—someone to help you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I keep taking the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just two more days of levofloxacin. Then you’ll finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Your lungs are clear, your abdomen is tender but not concerning, and you’re walking with your walker—great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for fixing the tube and helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your tube feeds slowly, use your inhalers, and call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or severe nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I have follow-up with GI and my regular doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all scheduled. You’ve done really well. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted for acute nausea, vomiting, and profuse green watery diarrhea, with a concurrent history of worsening shortness of breath and cough. Imaging revealed a new right upper lobe infiltrate consistent with pneumonia, treated with intravenous levofloxacin. A CT scan showed malposition of her GJ tube, with the jejunal limb pulled back into the stomach, contributing to her gastrointestinal symptoms. The tube was successfully replaced via interventional radiology. Diarrhea resolved after holding and then restarting tube feeds at a slower rate. She improved clinically, with resolution of respiratory symptoms and stable chronic pain management. She was discharged home with services on a 10-day course of levofloxacin, with plans for outpatient GI follow-up for esophageal stricture and continued management of chronic conditions including asthma, hypertension, and rheumatoid arthritis.
